entries.title: Small choice, big impact: empowering children’s digital resilience through nudging
entries.venue: Young Consumers Insight and Ideas for Responsible Marketers
entries.abstract: Purpose Children’s increasing exposure to digital environments raises concerns about their vulnerability to persuasive design and the psychological risks of technology use. This study aims to examine whether nudging, defined as subtle design interventions that influence behavior without restricting choice, can promote children’s digital agency and resilience. Addressing two central gaps in the literature, this study evaluates whether nudges undermine or enhance autonomy among young users and which types of nudges, reflexive (System 1) or reflective (System 2), are most effective for children’s positive digital behavior. Design/methodology/approach Study 1, a field experiment with 19 children (7–12 years) and 25 young adults (18–25 years), tested whether providing reflective choices slows impulsive engagement. Study 2, a large between-subjects experiment (222 children; 182 adults), compared three nudge framing conditions: re-anchoring, goal achievement and hedonic framing. Findings Reflective choice prompts increased engagement duration, while developmental patterns revealed that goal-framed and hedonic nudges enhanced perceived agency, decision comfort and prosocial intentions, particularly among younger children. Cognitively demanding re-anchoring nudges were largely ineffective. Originality/value The findings provide context-specific evidence that well-calibrated nudges can support rather than necessarily diminish children’s autonomy-related perceptions, offering a more cautious blueprint for designing digital environments that foster healthier and more intentional online behaviors.

entries.title: Intelligent Digital Solutions for Lifestyle Medicine: From Design to Deployment
entries.abstract: This book directly addresses a critical challenge facing the healthcare system: the escalating prevalence and cost of chronic conditions. The solution lies in harnessing the simultaneous, rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). The authors present a structured approach to designing, developing, and deploying intelligent digital health solutions to support the prevention and better self-management of chronic diseases, ultimately aiming to contain spiraling healthcare costs. This text provides a comprehensive guide to applying intelligent digital health to chronic care management. It first establishes the foundational essentials of digital health, detailing its socio-technical components, including crucial people, process, and technology aspects, and the indispensable role of AI/ML. Next, it deeply explores chronic conditions, emphasizing prevention and wellness management, while integrating key theories for supporting technology design and behavior change, such as co-creation, user-centered design (UCD), Task–Technology Fit (TTF), nudge theory, and gamification. The book champions a personalized approach, integrating precision medicine and genomics into lifestyle interventions. A significant highlight is the presentation of several real-world case studies demonstrating practical applications, including solutions for pre-diabetes reversal, a diabetes monitoring device (DiaMonD), a post-discharge cardiac rehab app, and an asthma management tool utilizing AI for trigger prediction. By focusing on orchestration and automation, the text shows how to ensure seamless data integration across multiple devices (e.g., smartwatches and sensors), providing evidence-based support for clinicians and empowering patients to take charge of their health. This book is an essential text for graduate and senior-level undergraduate students studying health informatics. For practitioners such as healthcare managers and IT consultants, entering the healthcare space this text would inform them of both the efficacy and importance of as well as how to design appropriate, effective, and efficient electronic healthcare initiatives.
